scripts/lib/slim.mjs, scripts/lib/usage.mjs and test/fixtures/slim are generated from the site repository (resources/js/lib/slimSession.ts, resources/js/lib/sessionUsage.ts), so the plugin trims sessions and counts tokens exactly like the site's upload page does. Change them there, then run npm run plugin:sync in the site repository.

API used: POST /api/v1/device/codes and POST /api/v1/device/token (browser sign-in, no token needed), POST /api/v1/imports (multipart: file, agent (claude-code, codex, cursor or pi), session_id, client_version, optional git (with commits.shas next to commits.subjects), usage, privacy (what the local check redacted, by type, and SHA-256 hashes of the values kept on purpose, never a value), continues, fork ({"session_id", "at"}: the session this one was forked from, and when; lines up to at are the original's), library ({"calls", "slugs"}: how often the agent called the library, and up to 20 slugs of the Builds it got; unknown slugs are dropped), trigger (manual or auto) and space: personal or a team slug; the response says where the draft went in space, the original's Build in forked_from ({slug, title, url}, or null while it is not on the site), and an automatic send of a session already published answers {"status": "skipped"}), GET /api/v1/imports/{id}, GET /api/v1/me (the account and its teams with their GitHub owners and whether each asks for automatic sending), with Authorization: Bearer <token>. The MCP server is /mcp (Streamable HTTP, the same token; mcp-headers prints it for Claude Code). Errors come as {"error": {"code", "message"}}.
content_text: Your coding agent forgets everything when a session ends. KeepPlain keeps that history, so you stop explaining the same thing twice. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi and Antigravity, and reads the sessions of GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Kilo Code, Cline, Junie, Qwen Code, Mistral Vibe, Factory Droid, Goose, Crush and Grok where they keep them. Free for personal use, teams pay per seat. curl -fsSL https://keepplain.com/install.sh | sh # macOS and Linux irm https://keepplain.com/install.ps1 | iex # Windows, in PowerShell keepplain login keepplain enable One file, no Node.js, no sudo. enable says what it found and asks before it changes anything. More ways to install What it does Find what you already solved. Your agent searches the sessions you sent to KeepPlain and opens the turn with the answer. /keepplain:resume picks a task up in another agent. Stop correcting it twice. Once a day a model reads your sessions and suggests the mistakes that came back in two conversations or more. Add one in a click and your agents get it at the start of a session or with the prompt it matters for. Rules Keep going at the limit. Past 90% of Claude's 5-hour or weekly limit, you get a button to continue in Codex or Pi. The brief is built on your computer without a model, and it needs no sign-in. Handoff See which session wrote a line. keepplain blame <file> is git blame with the agent session behind each line. Blame ● Claude Code · Harden the webhook 4 │ const TOLERANCE_SEC = 300; ○ Pi · Seat count sync 19 │ await syncSeats(event.data, { lock: 'team' }); ● Codex · maya, private 22 │ await markPaid(event.data.id, { notify: true }); no session found 25 │ return new Response('ok'); Learn from other people's sessions. Before a hard task, or when it's stuck, your agent can check the public library for how others got past the same problem. Library What leaves your computer. Sessions are sent only when you run /keepplain:build and confirm, or after you turn on auto mode. They are stored on keepplain.com as private drafts, and nothing is public until you publish it on the site. Secrets are replaced on your computer before anything is sent. That check works by patterns and can miss things, so read the preview. This plugin is MIT, the site is not open source. The full list Install From a terminal curl -fsSL https://keepplain.com/install.sh | sh # macOS and Linux irm https://keepplain.com/install.ps1 | iex # Windows, in PowerShell keepplain login This installs keepplain, one file with no Node.js needed, into ~/.keepplain/bin and adds that folder to your PATH (the rc file of your shell; on Windows the user PATH). The installer takes the file for your platform from this repository's releases and checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS. No sudo or administrator rights. KEEPPLAIN_VERSION=0.16.0 installs that version, KEEPPLAIN_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 leaves PATH alone. keepplain login waits in the terminal until you press Connect in the browser; over SSH it prints the link and the code to open elsewhere. keepplain update replaces the file with the latest release after checking its SHA256. A command you type mentions a newer release in one line, at most once a day; it never waits for the network to do so, and hooks never check. KEEPPLAIN_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 turns that off. Then keepplain enable connects Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Pi to it. It says what it found and what it will do, asks, and then installs the plugin through each agent's own plugin system: it lays the plugin out in ~/.keepplain/plugin and adds that folder as the local marketplace keepplain-local (claude plugin marketplace add, claude plugin install keepplain@keepplain-local; codex plugin marketplace add, codex plugin add), and installs Pi's package from it with pi install. Cursor has no command that installs a plugin, so it gets what the plugin is made of as files of its own folder, ~/.cursor, next to whatever is there: the hooks in hooks.json, the commands as skills in skills/keepplain-* and the library in mcp.json. Only what is ours is ever changed in them, and a file it cannot read (comments, a syntax error) is left as it is and the lines to add are printed. It is the same plugin as the one below, but its hooks and skills call keepplain by its absolute path, so no Node.js is needed and desktop apps find it without your shell's PATH. On the way it: replaces the plugin from the GitHub marketplace (keepplain@keepplain), or Pi's git package (pi install git:github.com/keepplain/keepplain-plugin), whose hooks would otherwise run twice; leaves the plugin from Claude's plugin directory (keepplain@synced) as it is, and says what it lacks. That copy has no hooks: alone, it gets no copy of ours next to it, so Claude Code has no auto mode, rules or snapshots until you remove it on claude.ai and run enable again. Next to a copy with hooks, that copy stays too. The directory's copy is removed on claude.ai, not by disable; finds a KeepPlain MCP server you added by hand (claude mcp add, mcp_servers in Codex's config.toml, an entry in ~/.cursor/mcp.json) and removes it, or keeps it and installs the plugin without its own server for that agent; asks once about auto mode for every agent it found (off unless you say otherwise). Codex runs the hooks only after you trust them in /hooks; enable does not do that for you. Cursor and Pi need nothing of the kind; in a git repository, asks whether to put the KeepPlain git hooks into it (no, unless they are there already; see Git hooks); asks once whether to import your sessions of the last 30 days to your private drafts (yes, unless you say no; see Past sessions). keepplain enable --yes goes ahead without asking, with --agent=claude-code,codex,cursor,pi, --auto=off|on|team|push, --mcp=remove|keep, --git-hooks, --no-git-hooks or --no-trailers, and --import-past (with --import-days=N) for the answers; without --import-past it imports nothing. keepplain status shows the file, the sign-in, each agent's KeepPlain plugins and auto mode, and the git hooks of the repository you are in. keepplain disable uninstalls the plugin and its marketplace from Claude Code and Codex, removes Pi's package, takes the hooks, skills and library entry it wrote out of ~/.cursor, and takes the git hooks out of every repository enable put them in; the sign-in, your settings and the file stay. keepplain update lays the plugin out again in the new version and updates it in the agents, so the plugin's version is always the file's. To send a session without going back into it, run keepplain sessions in the folder it ran in (or keepplain sessions --all anywhere, for every project's sessions of the last 30 days): it lists that folder's Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Pi sessions (also those run at the top of its repository), newest first, with how many prompts each has, the start of the first one and whether it was sent already. keepplain build 2 then shows the same summary and privacy check as /keepplain:build, asks [y/N] and sends; keepplain build alone takes the newest session, and a session id works too. It takes the same options (--private, --team=<slug>, --keep=<numbers>, --continues=<link>). It runs only in a terminal: neither an agent nor a script can answer its question, and there is no --yes. From a script, keepplain preview <id> and keepplain send <id> (with --agent=codex, --agent=cursor or --agent=pi for the others) do the two steps. A KeepPlain connector your organisation added in claude.ai is not visible on your computer, so enable cannot find it. If the agent then lists the library's tools twice, turn one of the two servers off in /mcp. Programs read the commands with --json: status, sessions, preview, send, discard, login, whoami, logout, enable, disable, auto, rules, nudge, privacy and import-past print one JSON object a line, the long ones an {"event": …} per step, and a failure as {"error": "…"} on stdout. The preview's findings come by number and kind only, never a value. login --json waits for Connect until the code expires. The desktop app KeepPlain app is a window over the same commands for macOS and Windows: a three-step welcome (the agents found, sign-in, enable, with a tick, on by default, for the import of past sessions), the agents with a switch each, the last session sent, every project's recent sessions (sessions --all) with a confirmation screen before each send, and the settings. It carries a released keepplain file and installs it in ~/.keepplain/bin when that one is missing or older. From Claude's plugin directory KeepPlain is submitted to Claude's plugin directory and not listed yet. The directory takes command hooks, header helpers and mods only from Verified organizations, so it gets a smaller copy of the plugin, made from this repository by scripts/directory.mjs: the skills and the library, without auto mode, git snapshots, rules in every session or the handoff offer, and without the commands that set things up (enable, update, the git hooks). It says what it runs and sends in its own README, and the directory reads it from the branch directory. Once it is listed: on claude.ai or in the Claude desktop app, open Customize → Plugins, find KeepPlain and press Add, then start a new session; the desktop app runs the plugin's scripts with Node.js 20 or newer. Claude Code in a terminal gets it too when it is signed in with the same account, as keepplain@synced. Then /keepplain:login as below; the library's tools sign in on their own, in /mcp. Keep one copy: next to the others it only repeats their commands. keepplain enable leaves it and puts none of its own next to it, and for the hooks you remove it on claude.ai and run enable again. From the agent In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add keepplain/keepplain-plugin /plugin install keepplain@keepplain Connect it to your account: /keepplain:login. It opens KeepPlain in the browser; check that the page shows the same code as Claude Code and press Connect. The plugin receives its token directly from the site and keeps it in ~/.keepplain/credentials.json, readable by you only. There is no token to copy, and it never passes through the chat. The sign-in request names only the program asking (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi or KeepPlain CLI) and its version, not your computer; the site lists the token under that name in Settings → Agent plugins. Needs Node.js 20 or newer, nothing else. Codex codex plugin marketplace add keepplain/keepplain-plugin codex plugin add keepplain@keepplain Start a new session, then $keepplain:login and $keepplain:build (the same commands as below, with $ instead of /). For the library, also run codex mcp login keepplain once in a terminal. Codex asks to run the plugin's command outside its sandbox: it needs the network to reach KeepPlain and your home folder for the sign-in. The session is found through CODEX_THREAD_ID in ~/.codex/sessions (or CODEX_HOME), and HEAD at its start comes from the rollout's session_meta, so Codex needs no hook for it. Codex runs the plugin's hooks only for auto mode (see Auto mode), and only once you trust them in /hooks. Cursor keepplain enable (above) is the way in: Cursor has nothing that installs a plugin from a script, so it writes the plugin into ~/.cursor, where the IDE and the agent CLI read it at every start. hooks.json gets four hooks (sessionStart, beforeSubmitPrompt, stop and sessionEnd, each running keepplain hook cursor <event>), skills/keepplain-<name>/SKILL.md the commands, and mcp.json the library. Restart Cursor (or run "Developer: Reload Window"), press Connect for keepplain in Settings → MCP, then type /keepplain-login and /keepplain-build: the commands below with a hyphen for the colon, since a skill's name in Cursor cannot hold one. Cursor's transcript of a conversation (~/.cursor/projects/<folder>/agent-transcripts/<id>/<id>.jsonl) has the prompts, the answers and the tool calls, but no tool results, no token counts and no time but the minute. The hooks add what it lacks: beforeSubmitPrompt and stop note the time of each turn, the model, the tokens of each answer and which conversation each workspace is in (in ~/.keepplain/cursor/: times and counts, never the text), so keepplain preview finds the conversation of the folder it runs in without being told. What each turn changed comes from the agent's own edit calls and the git snapshots. Cursor does not always call sessionEnd (a closed window, a crash): the next sessionStart sends what was left. Pi keepplain enable installs it with pi install. From this repository instead, without the file: pi install git:github.com/keepplain/keepplain-plugin That runs the scripts with Node.js, which Pi needs itself (22.19 or newer). Type /reload or start Pi again, then /keepplain:login and /keepplain:build. The plugin is one extension (pi/extensions/keepplain.js, named by the pi key of package.json). Its commands run in Pi's own process, so nothing of them lands in the session, and the question "Send this session?" is Pi's own dialog. Its events (session_start, agent_start, agent_settled and session_shutdown) run the same hooks the other agents have: auto mode, the git snapshots and the suggestion to share. The session is the file Pi keeps in ~/.pi/agent/sessions (or where PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR or the sessionDir setting put it); the extension tells keepplain which one, as Pi does for the commands it runs itself (PI_SESSION_ID, PI_SESSION_FILE). Pi has no MCP, so the extension registers the library's three tools itself; they ask the site through keepplain mcp-call with your sign-in. A fork (/fork, /clone) is a new file that names its parent: it is sent as its own draft, linked to the original. Pi reads a repository's own .agents/skills (where use puts a playbook) only in a project you trusted. One repository One repository serves all four agents: Claude Code reads .claude-plugin/ and skills/, Codex reads .codex-plugin/, .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, codex/skills/ and codex/hooks.json (its manifest points there, so Codex never picks up hooks/hooks.json; the same scripts run with --agent=codex), Pi loads the extension the pi key of package.json names, and cursor/skills/ holds the skills enable copies into ~/.cursor. Codex does not expand ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} or ${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID} in skills, so its skills give the script path relative to the skill file and pass --agent=codex. Claude Code on the web A session on claude.ai/code keeps its whole transcript in its cloud machine (~/.claude/projects/… there). Teleporting it to your computer brings only the part after its last compaction, so /keepplain:build there sends a long session without its beginning. The cloud machine installs no plugins, though, and reaches KeepPlain only when its environment allows it. So a cloud session sends itself another way, with nothing to set up in the environment: Connect the KeepPlain connector in claude.ai (connector settings). The same connector gives the agent the library. A connection made before connectors could send sessions can only read: disconnect and connect it again (the upload tools say so). Add the KeepPlain skill: download keepplain-skill.zip from the latest release and upload it in claude.ai's skills settings. Cloud sessions load the skills you enable on claude.ai by themselves. In a cloud session, ask: "send this session to KeepPlain" (or, with this plugin on your claude.ai account, /keepplain:build: in a cloud machine with no token of its own it takes the same route by itself). The skill runs this plugin's script in the cloud machine: it finds the session (the newest transcript there), shows what goes and what the privacy check found, and asks. Then the connector's start_session_upload hands out a one-time upload link (15 minutes) in the site's storage (Cloudflare R2, which the cloud's default network list allows), keepplain send --connector --upload=<link> puts the session there, and finish_session_upload makes the draft and returns its link. The skill is built by node scripts/skill.mjs (dist/keepplain-skill.zip: its SKILL.md is web-skill/SKILL.md), and each release carries it. The proxy of a cloud machine looks inside TLS with its own CA. The plugin trusts it from SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE, the system store (Node 22.15 and newer) or ~/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt, where Claude Code on the web keeps it, on top of Node's own CAs and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS. Where KeepPlain itself is refused by a proxy, the plugin says so and, in Claude Code on the web, which environment setting lets it through. Coming from Coders Talk KeepPlain was called Coders Talk until October 2026, and the plugin does not take the old one over: take it off first, or its hooks run next to the new ones. coders-talk disable takes it out of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Pi. Delete ~/.coders-talk and the # Coders Talk CLI line in your shell profile (on Windows, %USERPROFILE%\.coders-talk\bin in your PATH). If you added Coders Talk from Claude's plugin directory, remove it in Customize → Plugins; the Coders Talk desktop app, in Settings → Apps. The new plugin leaves the old blocks alone: delete <!-- coders-talk:… --> blocks in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md and # >>> coders-talk blocks in git hooks. Then install as above and sign in again with /keepplain:login (or keepplain login). Use Send the Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Pi session you are in to KeepPlain as a draft Build: the prompts, interventions and fails that mattered, with the raw log one layer down. The plugin never publishes. The draft is private: only you see it, or your team when the session ran in one of the team's repositories. You review every moment on the site and publish it there if you want to. The other way round, the plugin gives your agent the KeepPlain library: before a non-trivial task, or after a few failed attempts, it can look up sessions where other developers did something similar, and what went wrong for them (see The library in your agent). And /keepplain:use puts a published Build's playbook, what that session learned the hard way, into your repository as a skill or a rule (see Playbooks). The commands are the same in every agent, typed its way: /keepplain:build in Claude Code and Pi, $keepplain:build in Codex, /keepplain-build in Cursor. The tables below use the first. Command What it does /keepplain:build Shows what would be sent (project folder, prompts, time span, size), where it goes and what the privacy check found, asks, sends, prints the draft link. /keepplain:build --private The same, and the draft stays yours even in a team's repository. /keepplain:build --team <slug> The same, and the draft goes to that team (the part after /t/ in the team's link). /keepplain:auto on From now on every session of this agent on this computer is sent by itself while it runs and when it ends (see Auto mode). /keepplain:auto team The same, only for sessions in repositories of teams that ask for it. /keepplain:auto off Stops it. /keepplain:auto alone says whether it is on and what it last sent. /keepplain:auto session on Only this session is sent by itself, even with auto mode off. session off keeps this session on the computer whatever the mode; session alone says which applies. /keepplain:login Connects this computer through the browser, or says which account it is connected to. /keepplain:logout Forgets the token on this computer (revoke it on the site under Settings → Agent plugins). /keepplain:lookup <task> Searches the KeepPlain library for sessions of a similar task and shows what came back. The agent also does this by itself (see below). /keepplain:use <link> Shows a published Build's playbook as a skill for this agent: the whole text, where it goes and what changed since the version here. Asks, then writes it. --as rule or --as prompt for the other two forms; --team <team> --stack <stack> for your team's rules (see Playbooks). /keepplain:rules Shows the rules this repository's sessions get at their start, and why: its stacks, whose repository it is (see Rules in every session). on or off switches them for this computer; --refresh asks the site now. /keepplain:handoff [agent] A brief of this session for another agent on this computer, in your clipboard and a file, with the command that starts that agent on it (see Continue in another agent). on, off or a percent sets the offer the plugin makes by itself when a limit is near. Sending the same session again updates its draft until you publish it. Two rules: Commands that send your session (build and auto, and login and logout with them) run only when you type them. The agent never invokes them on its own (in Cursor their skills are marked so; in Pi they are extension commands, which only you can type). Putting a playbook into your repository (use) runs only when you type it too. The library may tell the agent that a session has a playbook; the agent can only pass that on to you. Searching the library is something the agent does by itself when a task calls for it (the lookup skill and the keepplain MCP server). It sends a short description of the task and the stack, never the session. Switch it off in /mcp (Claude Code), in ~/.codex/config.toml (Codex) or in Settings → MCP (Cursor); see The library in your agent. A forked session (/branch or --fork-session in Claude Code, a fork in Codex, /fork or /clone in Pi) is sent as its own draft, and the plugin tells the site which session it came from and where it left it. The fork's Build then says it is a fork and links to the Build of the original session, and the original's Build links to its forks. Whichever of the two is sent first, the link appears once both are on the site. Claude Code writes the lines the fork inherited with the original's session id and Codex names it in the rollout's session_meta and Pi in the header of the new file, so no hook is needed for it. Cursor's transcripts do not say whether a conversation was forked. If the privacy check found something the preview lists it by number; it goes as [REDACTED] unless you name its number, and the preview runs again with --keep=<numbers> (see What leaves your machine). If KeepPlain cannot be reached or answers with a server error, the send step opens keepplain.com/new in the browser and the file manager with the prepared .jsonl.gz selected, and prints the link and the path: drop the file on the page. It is the same checked file the preview described. It is kept for 30 minutes, so sending again once the site is back works too; after that the next run of keepplain (or the next session start) deletes it. KEEPPLAIN_NO_BROWSER=1 keeps the browser and the file manager closed; the link and the path are printed anyway. A rejected token or request never ends up there: sign in again instead. Auto mode Off until you turn it on, per computer, per site and per agent: /keepplain:auto on in Claude Code never sends Codex, Cursor or Pi sessions, and the other way round. With it on, each session is sent the way /keepplain:build would send it, without asking: to your team's space when the repository is one of your team's, else to your private Builds. With /keepplain:auto team, only sessions in repositories of teams that ask for it (a team setting) are sent, and nothing else leaves the machine. A team can ask; it can never switch this on for you. One session can choose for itself. /keepplain:auto session on sends the current session the way on would, even while auto mode is off for the computer; other sessions are not touched. /keepplain:auto session off keeps the current session on the computer whatever the mode, the git hooks' push included (what it already sent stays a draft). The choice is kept in auto-sessions.json with the session, so a resumed session keeps it, and /keepplain:auto off does not forget it. KEEPPLAIN_AUTO=0 still stops everything. These hooks do the sending, each in a background process so the agent never waits for an upload: Stop, after an answer of the agent: when the session grew and the last send is five minutes old, it is sent as still going. The draft stays up to date, and a crash loses at most those minutes. A session shorter than five minutes is only sent at its end. PostToolUse (Claude Code), after each tool call: the same check, so a turn the agent works on for an hour is sent while it runs, not only once it answers. Claude Code runs it without waiting for it (async), and it loads nothing but auto mode. SessionEnd: the session is sent once more, as ended. Codex also ends a session after 30 idle minutes, which is what ends one in its desktop app. SessionStart: sessions that never said they ended (a crash, a closed terminal) and grew since their last send are sent at the next start, up to three at a time. One quiet for half an hour goes as ended; a fresher one as still going. Only sessions auto mode saw while it was on, or turned on for themselves, are considered, never older history: that is the one-time import's (Past sessions). The site asks the model for moments when a session is over: when the plugin says it ended, or after half an hour without anything new. A session that goes on after that is asked about again at its next end, from the whole session, as long as you have not changed the timeline yourself. Sending a session that is still going costs nothing and does not count against the daily limit. A conversation in the Claude app can be several sessions: the app starts a new one, with the lines up to there copied in, whenever you edit a message you sent and when a conversation is continued. The plugin sends such a chain as one session, under the newest one's id, and names the sessions before it (chain), so the site keeps updating the one draft. A late send of a session the conversation already went on from is left alone (skipped: the conversation went on in a later session). Nothing is published by it. A session you already published is left alone. Every send gets a line in ~/.keepplain/auto.log: sent or synced (with the draft link), skipped and why, or failed. The log keeps its last 500 lines, none older than 30 days. ~/.keepplain/auto-sessions.json remembers which sessions auto mode saw and how much of each went, never their content; /keepplain:auto off forgets it. KEEPPLAIN_AUTO=0 in the environment turns auto mode off for that shell. In Cursor the hooks are the ones enable wrote into ~/.cursor/hooks.json (sessionStart, stop and sessionEnd, and beforeSubmitPrompt, which only notes the turn); nothing has to be trusted. The IDE does not call sessionEnd every time, so the site also asks for moments after half an hour without anything new, and the next sessionStart sends what was left. In Pi the extension runs the hooks on session_start, agent_settled (after an answer) and session_shutdown; Pi waits for the last one, so the upload starts in the background before it exits. In Codex the hooks are codex/hooks.json. Codex runs a plugin's hooks only once you trust them: type /hooks and trust the three KeepPlain hooks ($keepplain:auto on reminds you). On Windows Codex runs them through PowerShell and puts the plugin folder into ${PLUGIN_ROOT} itself. When the Codex CLI exits it also ends what its hooks started, so the session-end hook waits up to three seconds for the upload; what does not make it goes at the next start, and the site asks for moments after half an hour without anything new anyway. Past sessions Your memory starts empty: search_my_work and "why did this change" find only what the site has. Your agents still keep the sessions they ran before the plugin did (Claude Code about 30 days in ~/.claude/projects, Codex in ~/.codex/sessions, Cursor in ~/.cursor/projects, Pi in its sessions folder), so keepplain enable, the desktop app's welcome and keepplain import-past offer to import them. The import runs once per account: the site takes past sessions for 14 days from the first one, and after that the plugin no longer offers it. It finds the sessions of the last 30 days (--days=N, up to 90) with a prompt in them, quiet for half an hour, neither sent from this computer nor known to auto mode (sent.json, auto-sessions.json; a session you turned off with auto session off never goes), says how many of which projects, and asks [Y/n]. Without a terminal it asks nothing and sends nothing unless it is told yes: keepplain import-past start, import-past --yes, enable --yes --import-past (the app's tick). import-past --json says what it found, by agent and project, and whether the site still takes them. A yes sends them as auto mode would (auto-send <id> --past): the same slimming, the same redaction on this computer and privacy.json's words. They always go to your private drafts, whatever the repository; a team gets only those you share with it (below). The site takes them as trigger=backfill: dated by when each session ran, not when it was sent, labelled through the Batch API, and counted against an allowance of their own (100 a day, also after you share some with a team), never auto mode's nor the team's. An empty one is dropped without a notification. In the background, oldest first, one every 15 seconds (the site takes five sends a minute). When the day's allowance is used up, it stops until midnight UTC and goes on at the next agent session start, at keepplain login or at keepplain import-past. A busy site is waited for a minute; one out of reach, half an hour; a session the site keeps failing on is tried three times, then left out. A sign-in the site no longer accepts puts the import back to waiting for keepplain login, with nothing lost. A Claude app conversation of several sessions goes as one draft, as in auto mode. Auto mode leaves these sessions alone until you go on with one of them. A session's commits are those up to when it ended, on the branch it ran on when that is still here, not everything up to today's HEAD. Cursor's transcripts do not say which folder they ran in. The folder is the one of Cursor's workspaces (its workspaceStorage) or of another agent's session whose name gives Cursor's folder name; a conversation whose folder stays unknown is left out, and the count says so. Not signed in yet (enable before login), it waits and starts at the sign-in. Sessions that ran in repositories of one of your teams (its GitHub owners, as the site routes them) are offered to that team, one question per team, in a terminal right after the import's question (or at keepplain login when you agreed before signing in): "14 of these sessions ran in Acme's repositories. Share them with Acme too?" Yes by default only when your auto mode already sends this computer's sessions there (on, or team for a team that asks for it) and the team waits for no new consent from you; otherwise no. The desktop app shows the list with a tick for each. The ones you share move to the team right after they are imported (POST /api/v1/teams/<team>/sessions); one already imported, at once. Nothing moves into a team whose changed terms you have not agreed to. import-past teams --json lists them; import-past share --team=<slug> --stdin takes the ids that go ([] keeps them all private). Join a team later and the site offers the same in the bell and on the team's consent page, once for each lot. keepplain import-past status says how far it got and why it waits; keepplain import-past stop stops it, and what was imported stays in your drafts. ~/.keepplain/past-import.json holds the import's sessions (their ids, files, folders, project names and repository addresses, never what was said in them) and its counts; the lists go 30 days after the import ended. auto.log gets a line per session, as for auto mode. enable remembers a no and does not ask again; keepplain import-past asks again when you want it. The other agents Twelve more agents are served by reading their sessions where each keeps them. keepplain sessions lists them with the rest, keepplain build sends one from a terminal (the newest of the folder, a number from the list, or keepplain build <session id>; from a script, keepplain preview <session id> --agent=<agent> and then send), and keepplain import-past takes the past ones. No plugin goes into them. Nine of them run hooks, and on macOS and Linux keepplain enable puts KeepPlain's into the agent's own file (the table after this one); in the other three, and in all twelve on Windows for now, a session goes when you send it. Agent --agent= Where its sessions are Read GitHub Copilot CLI (and the Copilot agent in VS Code, which writes there too) copilot ~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/events.jsonl (COPILOT_HOME) the file Gemini CLI gemini-cli ~/.gemini/tmp/<project>/chats/session-*.jsonl the file, replayed: it is a log of changes OpenCode opencode ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db (XDG_DATA_HOME, OPENCODE_DB) opencode db for the list, opencode export for a session Kilo Code (the command line and the editor extension from 7) kilo ~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db (KILO_DB) kilo db, kilo export Junie (run with a task) junie ~/.junie/sessions/<id>/events.jsonl, state.json (JUNIE_HOME) the files Cline (3.0 and later) cline ~/.cline/data/sessions/<id>/<id>.messages.json (CLINE_DIR, CLINE_DATA_DIR) the file Qwen Code qwen-code ~/.qwen/projects/<folder>/chats/<id>.jsonl (QWEN_HOME) the file Mistral Vibe (3.0 and later) vibe ~/.vibe/logs/session/unified/<id>/ (VIBE_HOME) the last snapshot and the journal since it Factory Droid droid ~/.factory/sessions/<folder>/<id>.jsonl the file Goose goose sessions.db in Goose's data folder (GOOSE_PATH_ROOT) goose session list, goose session export Crush crush .crush/crush.db in each project, the projects in Crush's projects.json (CRUSH_GLOBAL_DATA) crush --cwd <project> session list, session show Grok grok ~/.grok/sessions/<folder>/<id>/updates.jsonl (GROK_HOME) the file The hooks, on macOS and Linux: keepplain enable (or keepplain enable --agent=<agent>) writes them into the agent's own hooks file, next to whatever is there, and keepplain disable takes them out again and leaves the rest as it was. Each runs keepplain hook <agent> <event>. A hook file of your own with the name one of ours would have (Cline's, Goose's) stays as it is: that one event then has no hook of KeepPlain's, keepplain status says only some are in, and disable still takes out the ones that are. With them, auto mode sends the agent's sessions as it does Claude Code's, the git snapshots of a session are taken, and where the agent puts a hook's text before the model your rules reach it. A file that cannot be read as JSON (comments, a syntax error) is left alone, and enable says so. Agent Where the hooks go Your rules in its sessions Auto mode sends a session GitHub Copilot CLI ~/.copilot/hooks/keepplain.json at the start and with a prompt when it ends Gemini CLI hooks in ~/.gemini/settings.json at the start and with a prompt when it ends Qwen Code hooks in ~/.qwen/settings.json at the start and with a prompt after its first turn, as still going: run with -p, it runs no hook at its end Factory Droid ~/.factory/hooks.json at the start and with a prompt when it ends Junie hooks in ~/.junie/config.json with the first prompt (the start's too: Junie takes no text at a start) when it ends Mistral Vibe ~/.vibe/hooks.toml, between two marked lines no: it takes no text from a hook when it ends Cline ~/.cline/hooks/TaskStart, TaskComplete no after its first turn, as still going Crush ~/.config/crush/crushrc, between two marked lines no when it ends Goose a plugin folder, ~/.agents/plugins/keepplain/ no when it ends OpenCode and Kilo Code take hooks only as a JavaScript plugin, and Grok's were not tried: nothing goes into these three. Revoke it in Settings at any time. Each network call, and what goes with it: Call When What goes POST /api/v1/device/codes, /device/token login The program's name (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi or KeepPlain CLI) and version; then the device code. No token, no computer name. GET /api/v1/me whoami, auto, share auto, the preview (to say where the draft goes) The token. POST /api/v1/imports, GET /api/v1/imports/{id} build/send after your yes; auto mode The slimmed, checked session; agent, session_id, client_version, trigger; the git context (GitHub origin, branch, commit titles, hashes and sizes, when each commit was made and its file names, a name holding a word of your list left out); token counts; the privacy summary (counts by type, hashes of kept values); space, continues, fork, library (count and up to 20 slugs). The token. /mcp the agent searches the library (in Pi through keepplain mcp-call) The query and the stack the agent writes, and the token. Never the session. /mcp start_session_upload, a PUT to the link it returns, /mcp finish_session_upload build in a cloud session (Claude Code on the web) after your yes, through the KeepPlain connector The same session and fields as POST /api/v1/imports, in one JSON file, put at a one-time link (15 minutes) in KeepPlain's storage (Cloudflare R2, *.r2.cloudflarestorage.com); the connector's own sign-in on claude.ai, never a token from the machine. The site deletes the file once the draft is made, or a day later. GET /b/<slug>/use/<format>.md, /t/<team>/rules/<stack>.md use via=cli, the agent, write=1 when it writes. The token only for a team's own Build or rules. GET /t/<team>/rules/<stack>.md, /t/<team>/rules/<stack>.json?since=<version> SessionStart (in the background, at most every six hours), use --team via=hook, If-None-Match with the version in the repository, the token. Only for repositories with a team's block. GET /api/v1/rules SessionStart (in the background, at most hourly per repository), rules The repository's stacks (laravel,php), its GitHub owner (acme, nothing for other hosts), the names of team blocks already in its files, If-None-Match with the last version; the token. Not the repository's name, path or files. Not with rules off. POST /api/v1/blame blame The repository's project key (a hash of its origin address, or of its path), the file's path, and for each of its commits (up to 300, a hundred a request) the hash, the file's name in that commit, the first line of its message, its Agent-Session trailer and when it and the file's commit before it were made. The token. Never the code. Not when signed out. POST /api/v1/limits limits share; with limits share on, at most once a day in the background Once per agent with samples (Claude Code, Codex): the agent, the plan (max_20x from ~/.claude.json, plus from Codex's sessions), the agent's version, the first and last sample's dates, how many samples and answers, and each window's fitted numbers: dollars and tokens per percent with their interval, the typical miss, the weights of token kinds and model families, how many steps were kept and left out. The token. Never a session, a prompt, a path or a session's tokens. GET /api/v1/share, POST /api/v1/share/attachments share The Build's slug or this session's id; after a change, the pull request's or the repository's address. The token. PATCH /api/v1/share/settings, GET /api/v1/share/pending share auto on|off; SessionStart with the share auto mode on (in the background, at most hourly per repository) The switch; the GitHub origin address of the repository. The token. gh pr view, gh pr list, gh pr edit (your GitHub CLI) share --pr after your yes; the share auto mode The pull request's new description, with the block. Your own GitHub sign-in: the plugin never sees it. GitHub Releases update, and a background check at most once a day from a terminal The request for the release, with keepplain/<version> as its user agent; nothing about you or your sessions. Credentials the plugin reads Two kinds, and each goes to one place only: Your KeepPlain token. Taken, in this order, from KEEPPLAIN_TOKEN, the plugin option token in Claude Code (sensitive, kept in the system keychain; empty unless you paste one), or what /keepplain:login saved for that site in ~/.keepplain/credentials.json (readable by you only). It is KeepPlain's own token and goes only to the KeepPlain site it was issued for, as Authorization: Bearer … on the calls in the table above (scripts/keepplain.mjs, scripts/lib/hooks.mjs). The plugin's MCP server gets it the same way: .mcp.json runs node <plugin>/scripts/keepplain.mjs mcp-headers at each connection, which prints the header for the server's own site (https://keepplain.com/mcp) and nothing for any other; not signed in, it prints {} and the server asks you to sign in through the browser. A proxy's user:password, when your HTTPS_PROXY (or HTTP_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, or on Windows the manual proxy in Internet Settings) has one. It goes only to that proxy, as Proxy-Authorization when the tunnel opens (scripts/lib/http.mjs), never to KeepPlain. Nothing else is read as a credential. Your GitHub sign-in stays with your gh, which the plugin runs for share; GH_TOKEN in .github/workflows is the release job's own on GitHub Actions and never reaches your machine. The desktop app reads no token itself: it runs the same keepplain. In the tests (test/), every token is made up (ct_kkkk…) and every home folder is a temporary one. What the plugin keeps on your computer ~/.keepplain (or KEEPPLAIN_HOME) is readable by you only: the folder and every folder in it 0700, every file 0600 (Windows keeps the user profile private instead). File What Kept credentials.json, login-pending.json The token per site; a sign-in waiting for Connect Until logout; until the sign-in ends auto.json, auto-sessions.json, auto.log Auto mode's choice, the sessions it saw (path, sizes, times), what it sent Until you change it; each session 14 days after it was last seen; 500 lines, none older than 30 days sent.json Sessions you sent by hand, with the draft link 90 days sessions/<id>.json Where a Claude Code, Cursor or Pi session ran and HEAD at its start 30 days readers/<agent>/<id>.jsonl, readers/<agent>/.sessions.json, readers/crush/.sessions-<hash>.json, readers/<agent>/.start-<id>.txt A session of another agent as the lines Claude Code writes: the whole conversation, as the agent's own file has it. The list of an agent's sessions its command printed (ids, folders, times); Crush keeps a database in each project, so one list per project. And, for an agent that takes a hook's text only with a prompt (Junie), your rules for the session's start, kept until its first prompt Written again when the agent's copy changes; gone 30 days after it was last written. The rules' file goes with the first prompt cursor/<id>.json, cursor/current/ What Cursor's hooks noted: the time of each turn, the model, the tokens, and which conversation each workspace is in. No text 30 days snapshots/<id>.json, .index The git snapshots of a session of an agent with KeepPlain's hooks: Claude Code, Cursor, Pi, Antigravity, and the nine other agents that take them. Off for a session whose repository is too slow for them, or holds your home folder 14 days nudges/ Where the Stop hook stopped reading, and the counts and slugs it found 14 days kept.json, privacy.json Hashes of values you chose to send; your words to hide Until you edit them share.json Whether the share auto mode is on, when each repository was last checked, what it did since the last start Checks 30 days; the notes until the next start shows them rules.json Per repository (by its path): the stacks and owner asked about, the rules' text the site answered, when; and whether rules are off on this computer Each repository 30 days after its last session; the switch until you change it rules-given.json Per session: the ids of the stack rules its prompts were given, so each comes once. Not the prompts 7 days enable.json, plugin/, update.json, nudge.json, handoff.json enable's answers, the plugin it lays out, the update check, the suggestion switch, the handoff switch and percent Until disable or the next enable/update handoff/<agent>-<id>.md, handoffs/ The brief of a session for another agent; which limit windows a session was told about 14 days limits/ limits install and after: samples.jsonl (the time, the first 8 characters of the session id and both windows' percent and reset, when a percent changed or ten minutes passed), last.json, enabled, chain.json and settings.json.bak (the status line you had), module/ (the status line's copy of the code), share.json (sending on or off, when it last went) Until you delete the folder; uninstall keeps the samples The preview writes <temp folder>/keepplain/<session>.jsonl.gz and .json (a private folder, private files): deleted after a send, when you say no (build, or the discard step of the agent's build skill), and otherwise 30 minutes after the preview, by the next run of keepplain or the next session start. What the plugin writes into a repository Git hooks and the Agent-Session trailer: only with keepplain enable --git-hooks (or a yes to enable's question) in that repository. .git/hooks/prepare-commit-msg and pre-push get a block between # >>> keepplain and # <<< keepplain; the trailer goes into the commits you make from then on. disable takes the blocks out; trailers already in commits stay in history. Snapshot refs (Claude Code, Cursor and Pi): refs/keepplain/<session> in the repository's .git, one per session, pointing at your HEAD; the snapshot commits, made from temporary indexes, are in its reflog (git reflog refs/keepplain/<session>), where git gc keeps them and git log --all does not look. Never pushed by a plain git push. The refs go after 14 days (see above); their objects stay in .git until your own git gc prunes them, which the plugin never runs. share --readme --write: the "Built with AI" section of README.md, between <!-- keepplain:repo --> markers. Not committed. use --write: the skill (.claude/skills/kp-<slug>/SKILL.md or .agents/skills/kp-<slug>/SKILL.md) or the rule block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, and .keepplain/uses.json: one entry per Build, format, agent and path, with the Build's slug, the version (hash), the format (skill or rule), the agent (claude, codex, cursor or pi), the path written, the time (at), and for a team's rules the team and the stack. Nothing else: no user name, no token. Commit it or add it to .gitignore, as you like. In the agents' own folders, only with keepplain enable (and gone with disable): for Cursor the hooks, skills and library entry in ~/.cursor (hooks.json, skills/keepplain-*, mcp.json); for Pi a package line in the settings.json under ~/.pi/agent, written by pi install. Configuration Setting Where Default Site address KEEPPLAIN_URL, or in Claude Code the plugin option url (asked when the plugin is enabled). In Codex set the variable in ~/.codex/config.toml: [shell_environment_policy] set = { KEEPPLAIN_URL = "https://…" }. Cursor's hooks and Pi's extension get the environment the agent was started from https://keepplain.com Token /keepplain:login saves one per site; KEEPPLAIN_TOKEN, or in Claude Code the plugin option token (kept as a secret), overrides it (for CI, or a token made in Settings by hand) none Data folder KEEPPLAIN_HOME ~/.keepplain Suggestion to share a session that used the library KEEPPLAIN_NUDGE=0 turns it off for a shell; keepplain.mjs nudge off for this computer on Rules in every session KEEPPLAIN_RULES=0 turns them off for a shell; keepplain rules off for this computer on Offer to continue in another agent when a limit is near KEEPPLAIN_HANDOFF=0 turns it off for a shell; keepplain handoff off for this computer; keepplain handoff <percent> or KEEPPLAIN_HANDOFF_AT moves the percent on, at 90% Proxy HTTPS_PROXY (HTTP_PROXY for an http:// site, ALL_PROXY for both), NO_PROXY for hosts that go direct. Lower-case names work too. An http:// or https:// proxy, with user:password@ if it asks; SOCKS5 proxies are supported too (socks://, socks5://, socks5h://). In Codex, if a variable does not reach the plugin, add it to set as above none: direct On Windows, when no proxy variable is set, the CLI and agent hooks read the enabled manual proxy from Internet Settings before each request. Shared and per-protocol HTTP/SOCKS5 proxies, ProxyOverride wildcards, ports and are supported; loopback stays direct. Machine-wide settings are used when the ProxySettingsPerUser policy is disabled. Explicit proxy variables and NO_PROXY keep their priority. Reading settings has a two-second timeout per registry query; missing or unreadable settings use a direct connection. An unavailable configured proxy reports an error without retrying directly. PAC/WPAD scripts are not evaluated by the CLI; use an explicit proxy variable for those networks, or the desktop app's Chromium resolver. Node's own fetch ignores the proxy variables, so the plugin opens the proxy's CONNECT tunnel itself. Some networks reset a direct connection to the site after the first 16 KB, which lets whoami through but not an upload; there the proxy is what gets a session out. The script reads the url option from Claude Code's own settings.json (pluginConfigs). It does not rely on ${user_config.url} in the skills or on CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_* variables: in testing, the desktop app left the placeholder unexpanded and the variable did not reach commands the model runs. Support, privacy and license Questions and problems: hello@keepplain.com, or an issue in this repository. Privacy and security reports: privacy@keepplain.com. What KeepPlain stores and why: the privacy policy. The rules for using the site: the terms. Every place the plugin sends something is in What leaves your machine; it talks only to KeepPlain, to KeepPlain's own storage for a cloud session's upload, to GitHub through your own gh when you share, and to GitHub Releases for updates. The plugin's code is under the MIT license (see LICENSE). Development npm test # node --test, no dependencies claude plugin validate . --strict claude --plugin-dir . # try it in a real session npm run build # dist/keepplain-<platform>-<arch>, needs Bun npm run test:binary # the command and hook tests again, on that file npm run directory # dist/directory: the copy for Claude's plugin directory Claude's plugin directory reads the branch directory, not this one: each release tag has .github/workflows/directory.yml put the output of scripts/directory.mjs there as one commit, after test/directory.test.mjs checks it against what the directory refuses and runs it laid out alone. That copy is the same program, with scripts/lib/edition.mjs changed so that it runs only what its skills run, and without the files that set things up. scripts/keepplain.mjs imports those files (enable, githooks, hooks, update, agents) where it uses them, so an import of one at its top stops the build. Its text is directory/README.md, and the wording its skills change is in SKILL_EDITS: a skill that stops saying it stops the build too. node scripts/directory.mjs --commit does the same by hand and pushes nothing. The single file is the same scripts compiled with bun build --compile (scripts/build.mjs): keepplain.mjs is its entry, and the hooks run as keepplain hook <claude-code|codex|cursor|pi> <session-start|prompt|stop|session-end> (scripts/lib/hooks.mjs; the scripts in hooks/hooks.json call the same code). The plugin enable lays out is made from this repository's skills and manifests, built into the file (scripts/lib/plugin.mjs): Claude Code's hooks in exec form (command and args, no shell), Codex's hooks and skills for PowerShell on Windows (& '…') and sh elsewhere, the MCP headersHelper for cmd.exe on Windows, Pi's extension with the program written into it, and Cursor's skills and hooks for PowerShell on Windows and sh elsewhere. Pi's extension is pi/extensions/keepplain.js and Cursor's skills are cursor/skills/*/SKILL.md (with <plugin> for the script's folder until enable lays them out); npm test preloads test/isolate.mjs, which points Cursor's and Pi's folders at a temporary one, so a test never reads or writes the real ones. node scripts/build.mjs all builds every platform: Linux x64 and arm64, macOS x64 and arm64, Windows x64. The file does not read .env or bunfig.toml from the folder it runs in. A tag keepplain--vX.Y.Z builds, tests and signs the files on each platform and publishes them with SHA256SUMS as a release (.github/workflows/release.yml). scripts/lib/slim.mjs, scripts/lib/usage.mjs and test/fixtures/slim are generated from the site repository (resources/js/lib/slimSession.ts, resources/js/lib/sessionUsage.ts), so the plugin trims sessions and counts tokens exactly like the site's upload page does. Change them there, then run npm run plugin:sync in the site repository. API used: POST /api/v1/device/codes and POST /api/v1/device/token (browser sign-in, no token needed), POST /api/v1/imports (multipart: file, agent (claude-code, codex, cursor or pi), session_id, client_version, optional git (with commits.shas next to commits.subjects), usage, privacy (what the local check redacted, by type, and SHA-256 hashes of the values kept on purpose, never a value), continues, fork ({"session_id", "at"}: the session this one was forked from, and when; lines up to at are the original's), library ({"calls", "slugs"}: how often the agent called the library, and up to 20 slugs of the Builds it got; unknown slugs are dropped), trigger (manual or auto) and space: personal or a team slug; the response says where the draft went in space, the original's Build in forked_from ({slug, title, url}, or null while it is not on the site), and an automatic send of a session already published answers {"status": "skipped"}), GET /api/v1/imports/{id}, GET /api/v1/me (the account and its teams with their GitHub owners and whether each asks for automatic sending), with Authorization: Bearer <token>. The MCP server is /mcp (Streamable HTTP, the same token; mcp-headers prints it for Claude Code). Errors come as {"error": {"code", "message"}}.

blocks.html_en: Codex

Start a new session, then $keepplain:login and $keepplain:build (the same commands as below, with $ instead of /). For the library, also run codex mcp login keepplain once in a terminal. Codex asks to run the plugin's command outside its sandbox: it needs the network to reach KeepPlain and your home folder for the sign-in. The session is found through CODEX_THREAD_ID in ~/.codex/sessions (or CODEX_HOME), and HEAD at its start comes from the rollout's session_meta, so Codex needs no hook for it. Codex runs the plugin's hooks only for auto mode (see Auto mode), and only once you trust them in /hooks.

blocks.html_en: Cursor's transcript of a conversation (~/.cursor/projects/<folder>/agent-transcripts/<id>/<id>.jsonl) has the prompts, the answers and the tool calls, but no tool results, no token counts and no time but the minute. The hooks add what it lacks: beforeSubmitPrompt and stop note the time of each turn, the model, the tokens of each answer and which conversation each workspace is in (in ~/.keepplain/cursor/: times and counts, never the text), so keepplain preview finds the conversation of the folder it runs in without being told. What each turn changed comes from the agent's own edit calls and the git snapshots. Cursor does not always call sessionEnd (a closed window, a crash): the next sessionStart sends what was left.

blocks.html_en: That runs the scripts with Node.js, which Pi needs itself (22.19 or newer). Type /reload or start Pi again, then /keepplain:login and /keepplain:build. The plugin is one extension (pi/extensions/keepplain.js, named by the pi key of package.json). Its commands run in Pi's own process, so nothing of them lands in the session, and the question "Send this session?" is Pi's own dialog. Its events (session_start, agent_start, agent_settled and session_shutdown) run the same hooks the other agents have: auto mode, the git snapshots and the suggestion to share. The session is the file Pi keeps in ~/.pi/agent/sessions (or where PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR or the sessionDir setting put it); the extension tells keepplain which one, as Pi does for the commands it runs itself (PI_SESSION_ID, PI_SESSION_FILE). Pi has no MCP, so the extension registers the library's three tools itself; they ask the site through keepplain mcp-call with your sign-in. A fork (/fork, /clone) is a new file that names its parent: it is sent as its own draft, linked to the original. Pi reads a repository's own .agents/skills (where use puts a playbook) only in a project you trusted.

blocks.html_en: • In a cloud session, ask: "send this session to KeepPlain" (or, with this plugin on your claude.ai account, /keepplain:build: in a cloud machine with no token of its own it takes the same route by itself). The skill runs this plugin's script in the cloud machine: it finds the session (the newest transcript there), shows what goes and what the privacy check found, and asks. Then the connector's start_session_upload hands out a one-time upload link (15 minutes) in the site's storage (Cloudflare R2, which the cloud's default network list allows), keepplain send --connector --upload=<link> puts the session there, and finish_session_upload makes the draft and returns its link.

blocks.html_en: Use

Send the Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Pi session you are in to KeepPlain as a draft Build: the prompts, interventions and fails that mattered, with the raw log one layer down. The plugin never publishes. The draft is private: only you see it, or your team when the session ran in one of the team's repositories. You review every moment on the site and publish it there if you want to.

And /keepplain:use puts a published Build's playbook, what that session learned the hard way, into your repository as a skill or a rule (see Playbooks).

blocks.html_en: Two rules:

sentences.en: Two rules:

blocks.html_en: • Commands that send your session (build and auto, and login and logout with them) run only when you type them. The agent never invokes them on its own (in Cursor their skills are marked so; in Pi they are extension commands, which only you can type).

blocks.html_en: • Putting a playbook into your repository (use) runs only when you type it too. The library may tell the agent that a session has a playbook; the agent can only pass that on to you.

Switch it off in /mcp (Claude Code), in ~/.codex/config.toml (Codex) or in Settings → MCP (Cursor); see The library in your agent.

blocks.html_en: A forked session (/branch or --fork-session in Claude Code, a fork in Codex, /fork or /clone in Pi) is sent as its own draft, and the plugin tells the site which session it came from and where it left it. The fork's Build then says it is a fork and links to the Build of the original session, and the original's Build links to its forks. Whichever of the two is sent first, the link appears once both are on the site. Claude Code writes the lines the fork inherited with the original's session id and Codex names it in the rollout's session_meta and Pi in the header of the new file, so no hook is needed for it. Cursor's transcripts do not say whether a conversation was forked.

It is the same checked file the preview described. It is kept for 30 minutes, so sending again once the site is back works too; after that the next run of keepplain (or the next session start) deletes it. KEEPPLAIN_NO_BROWSER=1 keeps the browser and the file manager closed; the link and the path are printed anyway. A rejected token or request never ends up there: sign in again instead.

blocks.html_en: Auto mode

sentences.en: Auto mode

blocks.html_en: Off until you turn it on, per computer, per site and per agent: /keepplain:auto on in Claude Code never sends Codex, Cursor or Pi sessions, and the other way round. With it on, each session is sent the way /keepplain:build would send it, without asking: to your team's space when the repository is one of your team's, else to your private Builds. With /keepplain:auto team, only sessions in repositories of teams that ask for it (a team setting) are sent, and nothing else leaves the machine. A team can ask; it can never switch this on for you.

blocks.html_en: One session can choose for itself. /keepplain:auto session on sends the current session the way on would, even while auto mode is off for the computer; other sessions are not touched. /keepplain:auto session off keeps the current session on the computer whatever the mode, the git hooks' push included (what it already sent stays a draft). The choice is kept in auto-sessions.json with the session, so a resumed session keeps it, and /keepplain:auto off does not forget it. KEEPPLAIN_AUTO=0 still stops everything.

blocks.html_en: • Stop, after an answer of the agent: when the session grew and the last send is five minutes old, it is sent as still going. The draft stays up to date, and a crash loses at most those minutes. A session shorter than five minutes is only sent at its end.

One quiet for half an hour goes as ended; a fresher one as still going. Only sessions auto mode saw while it was on, or turned on for themselves, are considered, never older history: that is the one-time import's (Past sessions).

blocks.html_en: The site asks the model for moments when a session is over: when the plugin says it ended, or after half an hour without anything new. A session that goes on after that is asked about again at its next end, from the whole session, as long as you have not changed the timeline yourself. Sending a session that is still going costs nothing and does not count against the daily limit.

blocks.html_en: A conversation in the Claude app can be several sessions: the app starts a new one, with the lines up to there copied in, whenever you edit a message you sent and when a conversation is continued. The plugin sends such a chain as one session, under the newest one's id, and names the sessions before it (chain), so the site keeps updating the one draft. A late send of a session the conversation already went on from is left alone (skipped: the conversation went on in a later session).

blocks.html_en: Nothing is published by it. A session you already published is left alone. Every send gets a line in ~/.keepplain/auto.log: sent or synced (with the draft link), skipped and why, or failed. The log keeps its last 500 lines, none older than 30 days. ~/.keepplain/auto-sessions.json remembers which sessions auto mode saw and how much of each went, never their content; /keepplain:auto off forgets it. KEEPPLAIN_AUTO=0 in the environment turns auto mode off for that shell.

blocks.html_en: In Cursor the hooks are the ones enable wrote into ~/.cursor/hooks.json (sessionStart, stop and sessionEnd, and beforeSubmitPrompt, which only notes the turn); nothing has to be trusted. The IDE does not call sessionEnd every time, so the site also asks for moments after half an hour without anything new, and the next sessionStart sends what was left. In Pi the extension runs the hooks on session_start, agent_settled (after an answer) and session_shutdown; Pi waits for the last one, so the upload starts in the background before it exits.

blocks.html_en: In Codex the hooks are codex/hooks.json. Codex runs a plugin's hooks only once you trust them: type /hooks and trust the three KeepPlain hooks ($keepplain:auto on reminds you). On Windows Codex runs them through PowerShell and puts the plugin folder into ${PLUGIN_ROOT} itself. When the Codex CLI exits it also ends what its hooks started, so the session-end hook waits up to three seconds for the upload; what does not make it goes at the next start, and the site asks for moments after half an hour without anything new anyway.

blocks.html_en: Your memory starts empty: search_my_work and "why did this change" find only what the site has. Your agents still keep the sessions they ran before the plugin did (Claude Code about 30 days in ~/.claude/projects, Codex in ~/.codex/sessions, Cursor in ~/.cursor/projects, Pi in its sessions folder), so keepplain enable, the desktop app's welcome and keepplain import-past offer to import them. The import runs once per account: the site takes past sessions for 14 days from the first one, and after that the plugin no longer offers it.

blocks.html_en: • It finds the sessions of the last 30 days (--days=N, up to 90) with a prompt in them, quiet for half an hour, neither sent from this computer nor known to auto mode (sent.json, auto-sessions.json; a session you turned off with auto session off never goes), says how many of which projects, and asks [Y/n]. Without a terminal it asks nothing and sends nothing unless it is told yes: keepplain import-past start, import-past --yes, enable --yes --import-past (the app's tick). import-past --json says what it found, by agent and project, and whether the site still takes them.

blocks.html_en: • A yes sends them as auto mode would (auto-send <id> --past): the same slimming, the same redaction on this computer and privacy.json's words. They always go to your private drafts, whatever the repository; a team gets only those you share with it (below). The site takes them as trigger=backfill: dated by when each session ran, not when it was sent, labelled through the Batch API, and counted against an allowance of their own (100 a day, also after you share some with a team), never auto mode's nor the team's. An empty one is dropped without a notification.

blocks.html_en: • In the background, oldest first, one every 15 seconds (the site takes five sends a minute). When the day's allowance is used up, it stops until midnight UTC and goes on at the next agent session start, at keepplain login or at keepplain import-past. A busy site is waited for a minute; one out of reach, half an hour; a session the site keeps failing on is tried three times, then left out. A sign-in the site no longer accepts puts the import back to waiting for keepplain login, with nothing lost. A Claude app conversation of several sessions goes as one draft, as in auto mode. Auto mode leaves these sessions alone until you go on with one of them.

Share them with Acme too?" blocks.html_en: The hooks, on macOS and Linux: keepplain enable (or keepplain enable --agent=<agent>) writes them into the agent's own hooks file, next to whatever is there, and keepplain disable takes them out again and leaves the rest as it was. Each runs keepplain hook <agent> <event>. A hook file of your own with the name one of ours would have (Cline's, Goose's) stays as it is: that one event then has no hook of KeepPlain's, keepplain status says only some are in, and disable still takes out the ones that are. With them, auto mode sends the agent's sessions as it does Claude Code's, the git snapshots of a session are taken, and where the agent puts a hook's text before the model your rules reach it. A file that cannot be read as JSON (comments, a syntax error) is left alone, and enable says so.

blocks.html_en: Each session is turned into the lines Claude Code writes and kept in ~/.keepplain/readers/<agent>/<id>.jsonl, written again when the agent's own copy changes; from there it is slimmed, checked for secrets and sent exactly as a Claude Code session is, with its file changes, its failed commands and its tokens. For the four agents that keep a database, their own command reads it (it has to be in PATH), asked again only when the database file changes. Inside a command the agent itself runs, the session is known where the agent says it: COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID, QWEN_CODE_SESSION_ID, FACTORY_SESSION_ID, AGENT_SESSION_ID (Goose), GROK_SESSION_ID, JUNIE_TMPDIR; the others say nothing, and the id comes from keepplain sessions.

blocks.html_en: What each agent's own record lacks stays lacking: Junie's log has no words of the model's between its calls and no content of a file it read; Goose's edits say what changed, not on which line; Droid and Vibe count tokens for the session, not for each request; Crush keeps only its last request's, so a Crush session comes without tokens, and its edits, like Goose's, without line numbers. Every reader was written against a session taken from the agent itself (live/capture.sh, with a stand-in for the model: live/mock-model.mjs), which is in test/fixtures/readers.

blocks.html_en: A draft is private: it is in your My builds, not in the feed, search engines or your profile. If you are in a team on KeepPlain and the session ran in a repository of one of the GitHub organisations the team named, the draft goes to the team's space instead: the team sees it, nobody else. The preview says where the draft goes before anything is sent; --private and --team <slug> override it. Publishing to the community is always a separate step on the site, and for a team's draft only if the team allows it.

blocks.html_en: The plugin brings an MCP server, keepplain (https://keepplain.com/mcp), to Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, and the same tools as the extension's own to Pi, which has no MCP. There are three, all read-only: search_coding_agent_sessions finds published sessions of a similar task, get_coding_agent_session reads one of them, find_coding_agent_failures finds where agents failed on a similar problem and what the human did. The lookup skill tells the agent when to use them (before a non-trivial task on a known stack, after two or three failed attempts, when you ask how others did something), what may go into a query and what may not, and to treat the answers as other people's experience: it never runs a command from them without asking you. When a session helped, it says so with the link.

blocks.html_en: • Signing in. In Claude Code the server uses the sign-in of /keepplain:login: .mcp.json asks scripts/keepplain.mjs mcp-headers for the token at each connection (headersHelper), so the token is in no config file and never passes through the chat. Not signed in, the server asks you to sign in through the browser in /mcp, which is the only way in the copy from Claude's plugin directory: it has no header helper. Codex runs a plugin's header helper from the session's folder with an empty environment, where the plugin cannot find its own script, so in Codex the server signs in on its own: run codex mcp login keepplain once. Cursor signs in on its own too, to the server enable put in ~/.cursor/mcp.json: Settings → MCP → keepplain → Connect. Pi's tools use the sign-in of /keepplain:login. Searching the library needs no account; signed in, the server also searches your team's sessions and lifts the guest limits: see keepplain.com/for-agents.

blocks.html_en: • What a search sends. The query (a few words about the task, or the symptom of a failure), the stack, and the agent's name. The agent is told never to put code, paths, repository, company or client names, hostnames, URLs or secrets in it. The site keeps the query text, the filters and how many results it found for 180 days, not tied to you or your IP address. The session itself never goes with it.

blocks.html_en: • Another site. The plugin's server always points at https://keepplain.com/mcp: the Claude desktop app compares the address it shows with the session's and does not expand variables, so a ${…} address breaks signing in there. For another site add your own server and switch the plugin's off: in Claude Code claude mcp add --transport http keepplain-dev http://…/mcp, in Codex [mcp_servers.keepplain-dev] with url = "http://…/mcp" in config.toml, in Cursor another entry in mcp.json. Pi's tools ask the site that KEEPPLAIN_URL names. Sending sessions still follows KEEPPLAIN_URL and the plugin option url.

blocks.html_en: • Which Builds your session used. When you send a session, the plugin counts the agent's calls to these tools in it and collects the Builds their answers linked to (/b/<slug>?ref=agent), up to 20, and the Builds whose playbooks the agent worked with: a kp-<slug> skill it ran (ct-<slug> before the rename; the Skill tool, or /kp-… typed in Claude Code; a <skill> block, or the agent reading the skill's SKILL.md, in Codex or Pi; /kp-… typed in Cursor), by the Build's link at the end of the skill's text. Cursor's transcript keeps no tool results, so from a Cursor session only the number of calls is known, not the Builds they returned. A playbook written as a rule into AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md is in every session whether it helped or not, so it is not counted. The preview shows them. The site links your draft to those Builds: "Used from the library" and "Built with the playbook from @author" on yours, "Helped N published sessions" and "N built with its playbook" on theirs, once yours is published. Only the count and the slugs are sent, not the queries: in the session itself each library call goes as the tool's name with [library call — not kept] in place of the query and of the answer. The count and the slugs are taken from the session file on your computer before that.

blocks.html_en: • A suggestion to share. Once per session, after an answer, when the agent got Builds from the library and the session changed code, the Stop hook shows you one line: "Your agent used 2 Builds from KeepPlain in this session. Share yours: /keepplain:build". It sends nothing, and it never shows with auto mode on. To read the session for it, the hook goes on from where it stopped the last time and keeps that place, the count and the slugs in ~/.keepplain/nudges/. Turn it off with KEEPPLAIN_NUDGE=0, or node <plugin folder>/scripts/keepplain.mjs nudge off. In Codex the hook runs only once you trust the plugin's hooks in /hooks.

blocks.html_en: • What the hooks module runs. hooks/handoff.tsx is a Claude Code mod. It reads only the usage figures of session.measure and, on a press, the session's id, and it runs one program: the plugin's own script, node <plugin>/scripts/keepplain.mjs (once keepplain enable has installed the single-file keepplain, that program instead). It runs it two ways and no other: handoff --targets --json past 50% of a window, which answers the switch, the percent and the agents found on this computer; and handoff <agent> --session=<id> --no-copy --json on a press, which builds the brief. That command reads the session's file, runs git in the repository for the branch and uncommitted changes, and writes the brief to ~/.keepplain/handoff/; the mod then puts it in the clipboard through Claude Code. Neither the mod nor that command makes a network request, and no token is read: nothing leaves the computer.

The env and credential files the plugin knows by their names: .env and .env.* (not .example, .sample, .dist, .template), *.env, .envrc, .dev.vars, .npmrc, .netrc, .pypirc, .pgpass, auth.json, credentials*, .git-credentials, id_rsa and the other SSH keys, anything under .ssh/, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, *.pfx, *.jks, *.keystore, kubeconfig, .kube/config, .docker/config.json, secrets.yml/.yaml/.json/.toml, *.tfvars, *.tfstate, *.tfstate.backup, .terraformrc, .htpasswd, application_default_credentials.json, local.settings.json, .vault-token, .s3cfg, .boto, *.kdbx, *.gpg, *.ovpn. For those the session keeps no content either: a tool call that reads, searches or edits one (Read, Grep, a Bash or PowerShell command that names it; in Codex a patch or a command that names it) goes with its output replaced by [content not shown, the file may hold secrets], and in Codex its input too. A file with another name is not recognised, so check the preview. In Claude Code, Cursor and Pi the plugin's hooks (in Claude Code scripts/snapshot.mjs) run at the start of a session, at each prompt and after each answer, and take a git snapshot of the working tree: a temporary index in ~/.keepplain/snapshots/, tracked changes and new files up to 1 MB, a tree chained in the reflog of refs/keepplain/<session>, a ref that points at your HEAD, so git log --all does not list the snapshots. Your branch, index and files are not touched, and a plain git push does not send that ref. The build step turns neighbouring snapshots into what the agent changed in each turn (Bash and subagents included), what you changed by hand between its answers, and the commits of each turn. A snapshot slower than 3 seconds turns them off for the session. Snapshots and their refs older than 14 days are removed at the next session start in the same repository, and whenever keepplain build, keepplain status or the pre-push hook runs there (see What the plugin writes into a repository). Without git, or in Codex, the diffs come from the agent’s own edits in the session.

blocks.html_en: • Secrets the privacy check recognises: keys, tokens, connection strings, passwords in URLs, email addresses, public IP addresses and internal hostnames that match its rules are replaced with [REDACTED:TYPE] on this computer, before anything is sent, in the session, the branch name and the commit titles alike. A check by patterns misses what it does not recognise (a password in plain words, a token of an unusual format, a client's name you did not list), and that goes as it is: read the preview, and the draft on the site before you publish it. A home folder in a path (C:\Users\you, /Users/you, /home/you) becomes ~, and so does the one in the dashed name Claude Code gives a project's folder (C--Users-you-code). Your user name on this computer, the one that folder carries, goes as [REDACTED:USER_NAME] where a listing or git prints it: the owner of a file in ls -l, of a process in ps, the name in front of an address in git log, user.name=. Anywhere else it is a word like any other and stays; list it in privacy.json to hide it everywhere. The preview lists each finding by number and kind, never its value; --keep=<numbers> sends one as it is, and only a SHA-256 of it goes to the site, so the site's own second check leaves it alone. Kept values are remembered as hashes in ~/.keepplain/kept.json. Words to hide in every session, such as client names or internal services, go in ~/.keepplain/privacy.json as {"redact": ["Globex", "billing-core"]}. The rules are the site's own (scripts/lib/privacy.mjs, generated from KeepPlain), checked against the same cases in test/fixtures/privacy.
